entities.name: La Scala
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Teatro alla Scala (La Scala) in Milan, Italy is the world's most famous opera house, opened in 1778 and named after the Church of Santa Maria alla Scala it replaced. La Scala is to opera what Carnegie Hall is to classical music or the Louvre is to art: the supreme institution that defines world-class achievement, where careers are made or destroyed by the response of its notoriously demanding audience.

La Scala was built by Empress Maria Theresa of Austria, who ruled Milan as part of the Habsburg Empire. The Neoclassical theater by architect Giuseppe Piermarini held 2,800 (now 2,030 after renovations). La Scala's premieres include Verdi's Otello (1887) and Falstaff (1893), Puccini's La Gioconda (1876), Catalani's La Wally (1892), and important works by Rossini, Donizetti, and Bellini — essentially the canon of Italian opera. Arturo Toscanini, who conducted at La Scala 1898-1929, established the modern standard of operatic conducting.

La Scala's social and political history parallels Italy's: the theater was damaged by Allied bombing in 1943 and its 1946 reopening under Toscanini, conducted free for a devastated population, was one of post-war Italy's most emotionally significant cultural acts. Maria Callas's triumphant La Scala debut in 1951, her legendary 1955 Norma, and her 1958 walking off mid-performance in front of the Italian president are among opera's most famous episodes. The current artistic director Riccardo Chailly continues La Scala's central role in world opera.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: La Scala is the world's premier opera house, where Italian opera's greatest works premiered and where Toscanini and Callas defined modern operatic performance — the institution that sets the global standard for operatic excellence.
